intro: The Prelude to Act I of Wagner’s Tristan und Isolde, WWV 90, is heard here in its concert version. It opens with a four-note phrase in the cellos that leads to the woodwind, and the motion by a single semitone in that opening recurs throughout the prelude.

sections.label: Intro · Cellos, then woodwind, after rests
sections.mNote: Cellos and woodwind exchange three rising phrases, separated by rests.

sections.label: A · Strings continue the phrases
sections.mNote: The violin melody continues over moving lower strings.

sections.label: B · Rising line in woodwind
sections.mNote: The short rising melody passes between woodwind and strings.

sections.label: Dev · Strings climb beneath the woodwind
sections.mNote: Quick string figures climb beneath longer wind notes

sections.label: C · Whole orchestra, rising line
sections.mNote: Brass and woodwind rise above rushing strings

sections.label: Link · Brass rest, timpani roll on E
sections.mNote: The timpani roll on E beneath shortening string phrases.

sections.label: Coda · Concert ending
sections.mNote: The prelude ends without the sailor’s song.

cues.title: Opening bars, Tristan chord
cues.text: The cellos rise from A to F. Woodwind enter with F–B–D♯–G♯, the Tristan chord, which moves to E7, the dominant of A minor. The A minor chord does not follow, and a rest comes after the phrase.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel, Vorspiel und Isoldens Liebestod, plate Part. B. 1544, p. 3, opening bars: https://hdl.handle.net/1802/13070. University of Texas analysis and score examples, https://www.laits.utexas.edu/tristan/prelude.php and https://www.laits.utexas.edu/tristan/motive1-3.php.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Opening woodwind line
cues.text: The opening woodwind line rises by semitones, G♯–A–A♯–B. Wagner repeats the shape at new pitches, and each statement reaches a little higher.
cues.evidence: University of Texas, Tristan Prelude analysis, first seventeen bars and the rising desire motif: https://www.laits.utexas.edu/tristan/prelude.php. This note describes the opening motif across its successive statements.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Violin melody, bars 17–22
cues.text: The violin melody continues without the stops of the opening phrases, over violas and cellos, and each new idea begins before the previous one has ended. Wagner marks the rising first- and second-violin figures ‘auf dem G’, so they are played on the G string.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf score, pp. 3–4; p. 4 marks the rising first- and second-violin figures ‘auf dem G’. University of Texas, bars 17–22: https://www.laits.utexas.edu/tristan/prelude2.php.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Liszt, 1854
cues.text: On 16 December 1854 Wagner wrote to Liszt about his planned Tristan: “I shall erect a memorial to this loveliest of all dreams”.
cues.evidence: Wagner to Franz Liszt, 16 December 1854, quoted in Robert W. Gutman, Richard Wagner: The Man, His Mind and His Music, p. 163; quotation and letter date reproduced at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tristan_und_Isolde.

cues.title: The ‘glance’ motif
cues.text: The melody known as ‘the glance’ is tied to a scene told in the opera. Isolde stood over the wounded Tristan with his sword. He looked into her eyes, and she could not kill him.
cues.evidence: University of Texas, analysis of the glance motif and its Act I dramatic origin: https://www.laits.utexas.edu/tristan/prelude2.php. The sword and wounded Tristan appear in the Act I narrative, summarised at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tristan_und_Isolde.

cues.title: Central ascent, strings and winds
cues.text: The string figures grow quicker as the wind phrases lengthen. Violin and viola runs climb beneath notes held by oboes, clarinets and horns. Small swells pass through the orchestra, and each new rise begins while another instrument is already moving.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf score, pp. 6–10, the extended central ascent: repeated wind phrases, lengthened notes and increasingly rapid string figures.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Climax before rehearsal C
cues.text: The woodwind’s rising semitones and the glance melody now sound together across the orchestra. Brass reinforce them while the strings rush upwards.
cues.evidence: University of Texas, Prelude part 4, annotated bars 74–83: https://www.laits.utexas.edu/tristan/prelude4.php. Breitkopf score, pp. 10–12, approach to rehearsal C.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Timpani roll on E
cues.text: The brass stop. The timpani roll softly on E while the strings and wind play short phrases over a thinning orchestra. Wagner marks the passage ‘allmählich im Zeitmass etwas zurückhaltend’, and material from the opening returns.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf score, pp. 12–13, after rehearsal C: E timpani roll, withdrawn brass, string fragments, ‘allmählich im Zeitmass etwas zurückhaltend’. University of Texas, return of the opening material in bars 94–106: https://www.laits.utexas.edu/tristan/prelude5.php.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First performance, Munich, 1865
cues.text: At the Munich première on 10 June 1865, conducted by Hans von Bülow, the lovers were sung by a married couple, Ludwig and Malvina Schnorr von Carolsfeld. Wagner had completed the score six years earlier, in 1859.
cues.evidence: Tristan und Isolde, composition completed in 1859; première history and cast, 10 June 1865, Munich, conducted by Hans von Bülow: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tristan_und_Isolde. The present Fulda recording is an orchestral concert version, identified as ‘Konzertfassung’ in its Commons metadata.

transitions.title: The violins extend the rising phrase
transitions.from: Intro · Cellos, then woodwind, after rests
transitions.how: The violins carry the rising melody into a longer phrase. Violas and cellos begin moving beneath it, and the bass changes note while the upper lines continue. The semitone steps of the opening remain, and rests no longer separate each phrase. On the following rise, Wagner marks the violins to play on the G string (‘auf dem G’).
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf score, pp. 3–4, connected string writing and ‘auf dem G’ directions; University of Texas, annotated bars 17–22, https://www.laits.utexas.edu/tristan/prelude2.php.

transitions.title: Brass withdraw over a timpani E
transitions.to: Link · Brass rest, timpani roll on E
transitions.how: After rehearsal C the violins fall from the climax in rapid runs. The brass stop, the bass thins out, and a quiet timpani roll holds E beneath shorter phrases in the wind and strings. Wagner marks a gradual slowing, ‘allmählich im Zeitmass etwas zurückhaltend’. The long rising line breaks up again into short phrases.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf score, pp. 12–13, after rehearsal C: falling violin runs, withdrawal of brass, E timpani roll and ‘allmählich im Zeitmass etwas zurückhaltend’. The separate concert-ending transition is omitted because the performed ending edition is unidentified.

composer.epithet: Composer who placed the orchestra beneath the stage at Bayreuth, hidden from the audience.
facts: Theodor Weinlig, Leipzig, 1831; then the daily work of provincial opera houses
Dresden court conductor, 1843–49 · Bayreuth Festival founder, 1876
Wrote his own librettos; published essays on theatre, music and politics
Thirteen completed operas, including the four evenings of the Ring
composer.background:
In 1839 Richard Wagner and his wife Minna fled Riga ahead of their creditors and took a storm-battered ship to London. He was twenty-six, an opera conductor with two completed operas and no real success. The sea passage stayed with him. A story by Heinrich Heine about a captain condemned to sail for ever became Der fliegende Holländer; its overture begins over a bare fifth, with horns and bassoons playing against the storm music in the strings. The Wagners went on to Paris, where he made arrangements for publishers and tried to get his music staged.

He grew up in the theatre. Born in Leipzig in 1813, he lost his father as an infant and moved with his mother into the household of Ludwig Geyer, an actor and painter in Dresden. Wagner wanted to write plays before he knew how to write music. He heard Weber’s Der Freischütz and Beethoven’s symphonies, and in 1831 he took counterpoint lessons from Theodor Weinlig. Posts followed in Würzburg, Magdeburg, Königsberg and Riga. Die Feen was not performed, and Das Liebesverbot, his operatic version of Measure for Measure, failed after one performance in 1836. That year he married Minna, an actress.
